caseno:
Writ Petition No. 167 of 1989 with Writ Petition No. 287 of 1989. 
Writ Petition No. 374 of 1990 and Writ Petition No. 644 of 1989.
lawyer:
M. Amir-ul Islam with Tania Amir and Shirin Sharmin Chowdhury, Advocates—For the Petitioners in all the four writ petitions.
Md. Kaiseruddin Ahmed, Deputy Attorney-General with Md. Altafur Rahman, Assistant Attorney-General — For the Respondent Nos.1-4 in all the four writ petitions. 
Zainul Abedin with Zakir Hossain Munshi, Advocates — For the Respondent No.6 in all the four writ petitions
MA Hannan with M Khaled Ahmed, Advocates — For the Respondent No.7 in Writ Petition No. 287 of 1989
parties:
Abed Ali and others  ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
3. The case of the petitioners in all the four writ petitions are that they were respective owners of the lands described in Annexure-A respectively in the four respective writ petitions and these lands were at first requisitioned under section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 on 29.1.1963 in Land Acquisition Case No. 159 of 1961-1962 hereinafter called as LA Case No. 159 of 1961-1962. Thereafter the Government decided to acquire these lands and accordingly notified the same for the purpose of acquisition under section 5 of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act of 1948. There is no dispute that the procedures required for requisition and acquisitions under the said Act were followed. Compensation was also assessed and was also duly paid to all the owners of these lands including the petitioners and the predecessor in-interest of some of the substituted petitioners in these writ petitions. It is also the accepted position that these lands were acquired for setting up a satellite town for settlement and rehabilitation of the people on the outskirts of Dhaka City. Although initially it was alleged by the petitioners that these lands were acquired for the purpose of settling the refugees arrived here from India, at the time of hearing this case it was not pursued and it was accepted by the petitioners that in fact these lands were acquired for the purpose of settlement and rehabilitation of people by establishing a satellite town there. It is then alleged by the petitioners that although the lands described in the respective schedules of the four writ petitions were acquired with other lands in the said LA Case No. 159 of 1961-1962 the lands described in the respective schedules of the four writ petitions were not at all utilized by the Government or by the agencies for which these lands had been acquired and these lands were left vacant and totally unutilized. It is further alleged that the petitioners are in occupation of these lands despite acquisition thereof and by constructing their houses, etc. they live there. The further case of the petitioners is that since the Government did not utilized these lands for the purpose for which these were acquired the Government is under an obligation to release these lands from acquisition. In all these writ petitions in the prayer portion it has, however, been prayed that a direction may be issued by this Court for the purpose of releasing these unutilized lands from 'requisition' and the word 'acquisition' has not been used in any of the prayer portions of these writ petitions, although admittedly these lands had been acquired after initial requisition thereof under the Act of 1948. It has further been alleged in the writ petitions that in fact the Government adopted a policy of releasing these unutilized lands in favor of the previous owners and in pursuance of this policy asked the petitioners to appear before the respondent No. 2, the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka with all necessary papers. In pursuance of the above instruction the petitioners in fact appeared before the respondents Nos. 2 and 3 with all their papers relating to these lands but no action was taken by the respondent to release these lands and ultimately the petitioners have come to know that they have no contemplation to release these lands according to the Government policy adopted earlier. 

 5. The respondent Nos. 1-4 entered appearance in all the four writ petitions and contested these writ petitions by filing separate affidavits-in-opposition contending that after acquisition of these lands under the provision of section 5 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 these properties has vested in the Government and the petitioners had been completely divested of their ownership and title in these lands and, as such, they cannot claim to get back possession of these lands as a matter of right. It is also contended that the petitioners have also received compensation for their respective lands acquired by the Government in the above LA Case No.159 of 1961-1962 and after receiving payment of compensation there is no scope for them to claim release of these lands from acquisition. The next contention of the respondent Nos.1-4 is that the disputed lands are being utilised for the very purpose for which these had been acquired and the work of setting up the satellite town and the work of settlement and rehabilitation of people are taking place since their acquisition and, as such, there is no substance in the allegation of the petitioners that these lands are unutilised and would also remain unutilised. It has been further contended by them that if any of the petitioners are in occupation of any portion of these acquired lands then such occupation by them is without any authority and as trespassers. 

 10. Before we enter into the merits of the case of the parties in these four writ petitions we like to point out certain technical errors and omissions in framing the writ petitions such as, in Writ Petition No. 287 of 1989 petitioner No. 2 Abdul Latif has prayed for releasing as many as 8 plots being Plot Nos. 5, 10, 29, 60, 66, 83, 87 and 90 comprising an area of 1.33 acres of land of Mouza Lalasarai, JL No. 273 as at Annexure-A to this writ petition. The petitioners have also filed the notice under section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 served on this petitioner while requisitioning his property under the said Act before acquisition of his property under the same Act. This notice under section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 as at Annexure-B to this writ petition shows that only one plot being Plot No. 83 of Mouza Lalasarai JL No. 273 belonging to petitioner No. 2 Abdul Latif was requisitioned and ultimately acquired. We have not been able to understand why along with this plot No. 83 seven other plots were included in Annexure-A to this writ petition by the petitioners against the name of petitioner No. 2 Abdul Latif. Such discrepancies are in almost in all the writ petitions and in respect of many of the petitioners. Be that as it may, for these technical errors in framing the writ petitions, the writ petitions cannot be knocked down holding that these are not maintainable, because, in spite of these technical errors we feel relief can be granted if the court ultimately finds the petitioners have been able to make out their case. 

 11. In all these writ petitions the basic facts are admitted. It is admitted that in LA Case No.159 of 1961-1962 the lands attracted in the writ petitions, hereinafter called as the disputed lands, were at first requisitioned under section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 with effect from 29.1.63. It is also admitted that thereafter these lands were finally acquired by the Government under section 5 of East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 with effect from 22.10.70. It is also not disputed that the Government paid compensation to all the respective owners of the lands attracted in LA Case No.159 of 1961-1962 and these owners including the petitioners received payment of their respective shares of the compensation. 

 12. Mr. Amir-ul-Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, has argued that the lands as described in the four writ petitions are still lying vacant and unutilised by the Government and are in possession of the respective petitioners of the four writ petitions. He has also argued that in view of the above situation, from equitable standpoint and for the purpose of enforcing the purpose of the Constitution of Bangladesh which its Preamble vows as securing economic and social justice for its citizens, should be returned to the respective previous owners by releasing these lands from acquisition. He has also drawn our attention to certain Government policy decisions in the matter whereby, according to him, the Government expressed its intention to release all unutilised acquired lands in favour of the previous owners and has argued that after announcing this policy decision the Government is not empowered to go back on the said decision and is estopped from doing so and, as such, this Court in exercise of its power under Article 102 of the Constitution may issue a direction on the Government to implement the policy decision as the said policy decision is completely in conformity with the vows of the Constitution-makers as expressed in its Preamble, that the Constitution would secure economic and social justice for all its citizens. Mr. Islam has also drawn our attention to section 17 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 wherein it has been laid down that no property acquired under the said Act should, without prior approval of the Government, be used for any purpose other than the purpose for which it is acquired and, if so used, or does not use it for the purpose for which it is acquired, the Deputy Commissioner may take possession of such property and has then argued that this provision has been enacted in the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 only to give effect to the above vows in the preamble of the Constitution to secure economic and social justice to all its citizens, by returning such lands to the previous owners. 

 13. Mr. Kaiseruddin Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney-General representing the respondent Nos. 1-4, has advanced a very simple contention submitting that since the disputed lands had been acquired by the Government under section 5 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act. 1948 these lands had been completely vested in the Government and the petitioners had been divested of their ownership, right and title therein and, as such, the petitioners have no vested right of any sort whatsoever in these lands. Consequently, according to the learned Deputy Attorney General, they cannot claim release of these lands in their favour as a matter of right. He has further drawn our attention to section 8B of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 and has contended that under the said section the Government could release any property from acquisition only before compensation was paid to the effected owners and after the compensation had been paid no acquired property could be released by the Government. He has further contended that the provisions of Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 having been promulgated long after the disputed lands had been acquired by the Government under the provision of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 and had completely vested in the Government, the provisions of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982, is not at all applicable. 

 14. Mr. Zainul Abedin, the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 6 in all the four writ petitions, has contended that the Government have already allotted some portions of the disputed lands to them for construction of quarters for their staff and they had already taken possession thereof and proceeded with some construction thereon and, as such, the allegations of the petitioners that these lands are still unutilised have no substance. 

 16. Since the disputed lands were admittedly at first requisitioned under the provision of section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 and then acquired under section 5 of the said Act let us first of all decide the legal effect of such requisition and ultimate acquisition of these lands. In this connection sub-section (7) of section 5 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 may be referred to but before doing so, it may be stated briefly that sub-sections (1) to (6) of section 5 lay down the procedure which, before an order for acquisition under section 5, were to be undergone. We do not like to elaborate the above sub-sections since it is not disputed by the petitioners that the procedures laid down in sub-sections (1) to (6) of section 5 for completing the acquisition processes were duly and correctly undergone by the Deputy Commissioner concerned who under the said section was empowered to effect acquisition. 

 "(7) The Government shall then publish in the official Gazette a notice to the effect that the Government has decided to acquire the requisitioned property. On and from the beginning of the day on which the notice is so published the requisitioned property shall vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances and the period of such requisition of such property shall end." 

 It is not disputed that the Gazette Notification as required by sub-section (7) of section 5 of the above Act was duly published in the Dhaka Gazette, November, 5, 1970 at page 148. So by operation of sub-section (7) of section 5 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 the above lands completely vested in the Government free from all encumbrances and from the date of vesting of the property in the Government the petitioners were completely divested of their ownership, right and title in these lands, so the petitioners have no legal right to claim release of these properties unless such right is conferred on them by any statutory provision. We have not been able to find any statutory provision conferring such right except section 8B of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948, which runs as follows :— 

 "8B. Withdrawal from Acquisition: When the owner of any property which has been acquired under section 5 is willing to receive back the property, the Government may, at any time before the payment of compensation, withdraw from the acquisition of any such property by notification published in the Official Gazette, and on such withdrawal, the property shall be restored to the possession of the owner, and with effect from the date of such restoration, the property shall vest back in the owner the rights which he had before such property was acquired. 

 "A close reading of the above provision shows that when the owner of any property which had been acquired under section 5 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948, was willing to receive back the property, the Government might, at any time before compensation was paid, withdraw from the acquisition of any such property. The section appears to confer full discretionary power on the Government either to withdraw from acquisition or not, if any owner of acquired property expressed willingness to receive backs such acquired property. The said section did not impose on the Government absolute liability to release such property in case the owner of the acquired property was willing to receive back the property. This is absolutely clear from the word "may" occurring after the word "Government" in the said section. The second condition was that the Government was also empowered to release such property if compensation had not been paid to the affected owners. So this section did not confer absolute right on the petitioners to get back the acquired property, on the other hand, it was left to the discretion of the Government either to release such property or not. Moreover, such withdrawal from acquisition could not be affected if compensation had already been paid to the affected owners. In the present case, admittedly compensation had already been paid to the affected owners and, as such, the question of applying section 8B of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 could not arise. Similar view was taken by this Court in two similar cases in Writ Petition Nos. 526 of 1992 and 146 of 1989 and this view was affirmed by the learned Appellate Division of this Court in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 249 and 255 of 1993. 

 17. Moreover, since the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 is no longer in existence having expired on 15th August, 1982 (section 1(4) of the said Act read with the notification published in the Dacca Gazette (Extraordinary) dated 16th August, 1948, whereby this Act came into force on 16th August 1948) section 8B thereof cannot be applied now for releasing the disputed properties. 

 21. It further appears from section 17 of the Ordinance that the said Ordinance has not conferred any right on the owners of the acquired lands but simply empowers the Deputy Commissioner to take possession of such acquired lands as are left unutilised or are not utilised for the purpose for which they have been acquired. There is nothing in the section to show that after resuming possession of such unutilised lands the Deputy Commissioner or, so to say, the Government will be under any liability to return the lands to the previous owners. It appears to us that the manner of dealing with such resumed land has been left completely to the discretion of the Government and the Government in its discretion can also hand over these lands to the previous owners or to utilise these lands for any public purpose. As such, we are unable to subscribe to the view expressed by Mr. Islam that in view of section 17 of the Ordinance the Government is under a legal liability to return the disputed lands to the petitioners. 

 23. In answer to the above contention of Mr. Islam it can be said that in its writ jurisdiction conferred by Article 102 of the Constitution, the object set forth in the Preamble cannot be enforced although the Preamble can be used as an aid to interpretation of the Constitution or any other statutory provision if there is any equivocality or ambiguity in such provision of the Constitution or such statute. Article 102 of the Constitution empowers this Court to issue mandate only for enforcement of fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution (clause (1) of Article 102) and also to compel a person performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority to do which he is required by law to do (clause (2) of Article 102). The power to issue mandate or any writ in the nature of mandamus is, therefore, limited by the purposes mentioned in clauses (1) and (2) of Article 102 of the Constitution, Consequently, this Court in its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution cannot issue a writ for enforcement of an equitable right, because, this court while exercising its power under Article 102 of the Constitution, is not a Court of Equity. Moreover, assuming that it will be most inequitable and repugnant to the concept of social justice to acquire private properties of citizens, it may be pointed out that the said concept of equity and social justice enshrined in the Preamble to the Constitution is hedged in by Article 42 of the Constitution as well as Article 47 of the Constitution. Article 42 of the Constitution has guaranteed the right to property of every citizen on the one hand and immediately thereafter by enacting clause (2) has put restriction on the right of an individual to enjoy his property by authorizing the Government to nationalize, acquire and requisition private property and also laying down that no law enacted relating to the acquisition, nationalization or requisition of private property can be called in question in any Court even on the ground that any provision in such law relating to payment of compensation is inadequate in any Court. In addition to enacting Article 42(2) of the Constitution, the makers of the Constitution have provided that no law relating to compulsory acquisition, nationalization or requisition of any property can be called in question and can be deemed to be void even on the ground that such law is inconsistent with or takes away any of the fundamental rights guaranteed in Part III of the Constitution. As such, however inequitable the principle of acquisition of private property may seem to appear the above provisions of the Constitution itself have provided that such inequity cannot be remedied by the Court. 

 24. Last of all, Mr. Islam has drawn our attention to certain decision of the Government whereby the Government expressed its intention to release such acquired properties as are left unutilised or are not utilised for the purpose for which such properties had been acquired and has argued that the Government is bound by this decision. In this connection, Mr. Islam has referred to certain communication and certain news-items appearing in newspapers. The first communication to which Mr. Islam has referred is a semi-official letter from the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms to all the Secretaries to the Government. This letter is at Annexure-C to Writ Petition No.167 of 1989. A perusal of this letter shows that the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms observed that since the area of land in Bangladesh is very limited it is necessary to utilise every inch of such land. It has also been observed that many agencies get private lands acquired for various public purposes but do not utilise these lands and leave these lands unutilised for years together. It was then suggested that land in excess of what is absolutely necessary for the purpose for which it is acquired should not be acquired and, lastly, it was informed that the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms had taken a decision that if any land was left unutilised for more than a reasonable period of time such land would be released from acquisition and would be returned to the previous owners. Mr. Islam has also referred to another semi-official letter addressed by the Hon'ble Minister of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms to all the other Hon'ble Ministers. In these letter also similar observations as in the letter as at Annexure-G were made and the Hon'ble Ministers to whom this letter was addressed were requested to surrender the land left unutilised in favour of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms. There is, however, nothing in this letter to show that the Government intended to return the lands to the previous owners. Mr. Islam has then referred to another news item published in the Bangladesh Observer, dated 23rd August, 1983 as at Annexure-C 1 to the writ petition. In this news item news was published to the effect that the Government had decided to return unutilised lands to the respective affected owners and accordingly, according to this news item, the District Administration, Dhaka requested all the previous owners to bring to its notice all cases of unutilised lands. 

 25. From the above it appears that the Government was considering a proposal for returning unutilised lands to the previous owners. It also appears that in this respect, the Government also took certain steps and called for certain particulars of such unutilised lands. We have now to see whether such proposal and such decision taken by the Government have vested any right in the petitioner to get the disputed lands released. It appears to us that the above decision or proposal of the Government was an internal matter of the Government and the Government had been considering the said proposal. It also appears that the said proposal of the Government did not mature into any enactment or rule or even notification or final decision to return the unutilised acquired lands to the previous owners. Consequently, we find that on the basis of such proposal pending for consideration of the Government no right was created in the petitioners to claim back the disputed lands which had vested in the Government by operation of law. Moreover, it appears to us that even if such decision to return such land to the previous owners had been finally taken, it would remain the sole discretion of the Government as to which land should be returned and which land should be retained in its possession. To our view, such decision and such proposal cannot create any right in the petitioners to claim back the acquired lands which previously belonged to them. We are also of the view that the said proposal and the said internal decision of the Government cannot act as estoppel to prevent the Government from altering the decision. We are also of the view that no mandate can be issued by this Court in its power under Article 102(2) of the Constitution to direct the Government to implement the aforesaid proposal expressed in the letter as at Annexure-C and the news item, Annexure-C1. 

 26. The petitioners have alleged that the disputed lands were acquired for the purpose of settlement and rehabilitation of people by establishing a satellite town but even more than 30 years after the Government took possession of these lands large areas of these lands are still lying vacant. In reply to this the contesting respondents contended that these lands are being utilised step by step. It has also been averred in the affidavit-in-opposition sworn by the respondent No. 6 in Writ Petition No. 167 of 1989 that they have taken possession of the portion of the disputed lands which had been allotted to them and they have preceded with the work of construction of their staff quarters. Similarly, the respondent No. 7 in Writ Petition No. 287 of 1989 have averred in their affidavit in opposition that they have also taken possession of that portion of the disputed land which had been allotted to them and they have proceeded with the work constructing quarters for their staff to some extent. These facts are not disputed by the petitioners. Moreover, in a supplementary-affidavit sworn by the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 167 of 1989 a report of enquiry made by the office of the Deputy Commissioner Dhaka has been produced. This report is at Annexure-Kha to the supplementary-affidavit sworn on 19.7.95. This report shows that some of the plots are vacant and in these lands there are still houses in which some of the petitioners live. It has also been stated that various portions of the disputed lands had been utilised by various organizations to whom these lands had been allotted. It appears to us that these lands are being allotted to various organization’s from time to time and the establishment of satellite town for settlement and rehabilitation of people are taking place step by step. It, therefore, appears to us that the allegations that these lands are not likely to be utilised for the purpose for which these had been acquired, is not correct.
